passage:
Sunday. In the quiet before dinner, Jyoti taught her son Rafiq a game: smell the flower, blow out the candle. They did it five times, giggling. She also showed him where the water jug stood.
Wednesday. Rafiq lost at carrom, flung the striker and stomped off. Jyoti did not chase him or say "calm down." She waited.
Saturday. Rafiq lost again. His face went red. Then he walked to the jug, drank a glass of water, stepped onto the balcony and took five slow breaths. When he came back he said, "I'm still annoyed, but I'm okay. Rematch?"

qa.q: What game did Jyoti teach Rafiq on Sunday?
qa.a: Smell the flower, blow out the candle.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he flung the striker on Wednesday?
qa.a: Angry and frustrated at losing the carrom game, which is why he stomped off.

qa.q: What did Jyoti choose not to do on Wednesday, and why might that matter?
qa.a: She did not chase him or tell him to calm down. The skill had been taught on a calm Sunday, so she trusted him to use it.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel watching Rafiq on Saturday?
qa.a: Probably proud and relieved, since Rafiq drinks water, steps out and breathes without being told.

grounding: A child practises slowing breathing and drinking water while calm, then uses it after being upset.

passage:
Wasim, come and sit with your Dada Suraj. When I was your age I had a temper like a firecracker. One day at the tea stall I threw my slate because I couldn't do a sum. My mother didn't shout. That evening, when I was calm, she showed me: "When the anger comes, drink water slowly and step outside for a minute."
I laughed. But the next time I lost a game of marbles, I remembered. I drank from the earthen pot, walked to the neem tree and counted my breaths. The anger drained away like water through sand.
She never told me in the moment I was furious. Only before. That's why it worked.

qa.q: What did Suraj throw at the tea stall?
qa.a: His slate.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when he lost the game of marbles?
qa.a: Angry, like a firecracker, but he remembered his mother's words and let the anger drain away.

qa.q: What choice did young Suraj make when he lost at marbles?
qa.a: He drank water from the earthen pot, walked to the neem tree and counted his breaths.

qa.q: Why did Suraj's mother speak to him in the evening and not in the moment?
qa.a: She waited until he was calm, when he could listen, so the skill was ready before the next storm.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to drink water and step outside when angry, taught before the storm.

passage:
On Sunday at practice, Farhan Sir taught the under-12 team balloon breaths: in through the nose for four, out through the mouth for six. "Practise when you're calm," he said, "so your body knows it when you're not." Rashmi practised every night before bed, feeling a bit silly.
On Thursday the interschool match was moved to a muddy ground in pouring rain. In the second half, the referee gave a penalty against Rashmi that she was sure was wrong. Her face went hot, and she wanted to kick the ball into the stands.
Then her body remembered. In for four. Out for six. She walked to the sideline, drank water and did it three more times. When she came back on, her legs felt steady, and she won the ball twice before full time.

qa.q: How long did Farhan Sir say to breathe out?
qa.a: Out through the mouth for six.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling after the penalty?
qa.a: Rashmi felt hot with anger, sure the call was wrong and wanting to kick the ball into the stands.

qa.q: Why did the balloon breaths work on Thursday?
qa.a: Rashmi had practised them every night while calm, so her body remembered them in the storm.

qa.q: What might Farhan Sir feel watching Rashmi walk to the sideline?
qa.a: Farhan Sir likely felt proud and relieved that the practice worked when it mattered.

grounding: Shows a child using a breathing skill practised in calm moments to settle after being upset.

passage:
Jagdish lost the carrom final in the building's summer tournament to a boy two years younger. His hands started shaking, and he felt the old urge to flip the board.
Instead he did what his Dadi had practised with him on quiet evenings for months: walk out, drink water, count ten cars. He went to the gate of the Ahmedabad society, gulped from his bottle and counted. Red car, auto, bus, scooter...
Imran Uncle from the third floor, who ran the tournament, watched from the steps. By the tenth car, Jagdish's jaw had loosened. He came back in, shook the winner's hand and said, "Rematch tomorrow?"
Imran Uncle gave him a small nod.

qa.q: What did Jagdish count at the gate?
qa.a: Ten cars.

qa.q: How was Jagdish feeling right after losing?
qa.a: Jagdish felt angry and shaky, with the urge to flip the board.

qa.q: Why did Dadi's method work in the moment?
qa.a: They had practised it on quiet evenings for months, so Jagdish could use it without thinking when upset.

qa.q: What might Imran Uncle's nod mean?
qa.a: It suggests Imran Uncle respected how Jagdish calmed down and handled losing.

grounding: Shows a child using a calming routine learned in quiet times to step outside and settle after losing.

passage:
"Chandrika, before dinner, can we make a plan?" Deepika patted the sofa. "For the next time you get really angry."
"I'm not angry now."
"That's why now is the best time. What helps you?"
Chandrika thought. "Maybe cold water. And the balcony."
"Okay. Water, balcony, then you come and tell me. Let's try it once, pretend."
Chandrika rolled her eyes but walked to the balcony, drank from the steel glass, and came back grinning. "Done."
Two days later her brother tore her drawing. Chandrika's fists clenched. She opened her mouth to shout. Then she turned, went to the balcony, drank water and stood there a while. When she came back her voice shook, but she said, "Mumma, he tore it."
"Thank you for coming to tell me," Deepika said.

qa.q: What did Chandrika choose to help her calm down?
qa.a: Cold water and the balcony.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when her brother tore the drawing?
qa.a: Chandrika felt furious, fists clenched, ready to shout.

qa.q: Why did Deepika make the plan before dinner, when Chandrika wasn't angry?
qa.a: Calming steps learned and practised before a storm are much easier to use during one.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel when Chandrika comes to tell her?
qa.a: Deepika likely feels proud and relieved that the plan worked.

grounding: Shows a calming plan made and practised when the child is calm, then used after being upset.

passage:
I'm Arohi, and I used to explode when my little brother wrecked my things. I'd scream, throw stuff, cry for an hour.
One quiet Sunday, when I wasn't angry at all, my big cousin Raghav taught me three things. "When you feel it coming, breathe out slowly like blowing a candle, five times. Drink a glass of water. Step outside for a minute." We practised them on the balcony like a game.
Two weeks later my brother tore my comic. I felt the heat rising. And I remembered the candle. I blew out five slow breaths, drank water, went out on the balcony.
I was still angry. But not exploding angry. When I came back, I told him, "That was my favourite comic," and he said sorry.
I think it worked because I learned it on a calm day.

qa.q: How many slow breaths did Raghav tell Arohi to take?
qa.a: Raghav said to breathe out slowly like blowing a candle, five times.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when the comic was torn?
qa.a: Arohi felt anger heating up, but after the breaths it softened to plain anger instead of an explosion.

qa.q: Why did Raghav's calming steps work?
qa.a: They were taught and practised on a calm day like a game, so Arohi could remember them when upset.

qa.q: What would change if Raghav had taught the steps during one of Arohi's explosions?
qa.a: Arohi would likely have been too upset to listen, and the steps might have felt like being told off.

grounding: A child learns calming steps on a calm day and uses them when upset, since skills taught before the storm work better.
